title: Predicting the effects of solar energy development on plants and wildlife in the Desert Southwest, United States
abstract: Utility-scale solar energy (USSE) is rapidly expanding and expected to compose the largest source of renewablegenerated electricity in the United States and globally over the coming decades. Lands in the hot Desert Southwest (Chihuahuan, Mojave, Sonoran, and San Joaquin Deserts) are increasingly selected for USSE development because of their high solar irradiance. The Desert Southwest supports high biodiversity and provides many ecosystem services but is vulnerable to USSE disturbance and simultaneous stress from aridification and other growing land-use pressures. In this review, a framework is presented for predicting the effects of USSE development on plants and wildlife by linking disturbance types associated with USSE construction and operation to the traits and response strategies of species and guilds. Case studies from representative Desert Southwest species and guilds of conservation concern are used to: review known effects of USSE, predict unknown effects with the trait-based framework, and discuss mitigation strategies. This framework predicts that species with trait plasticity and broad ecological niches will be capable of exploiting USSE development, while species with specific habitat requirements and narrow niches will be more vulnerable. Opportunities for mitigation during development and operation that may lessen these effects are identified. This work is intended to inform USSE management decision-making and long-term planning, as well as encourage new research to test predicted effects and responses.

## **1. Introduction**

In the United States (USA), an energy transition is underway to significantly decarbonize the electrical grid by 2035 and reach net-zero emissions by 2050 [1]. Renewable energy is paramount to this transition, and its capacity to meet increasing consumer needs has grown considerably in recent years [2]. Growth in renewable energy development is largely being driven by solar energy, with projections for it to overtake both natural gas and coal to become the largest contributor to power capacity in the world by 2027 [3]. Electricity generated by solar and other renewables is forecasted to increase by 26 % in 2024, with utility-scale ( _>_ 1 MW capacity) photovoltaic (PV) solar constituting two-thirds of this near-term forecast [2]. In the long term, utility-scale PV solar is projected to represent over 80 % of the solar-generated electricity capacity to satisfy the 2050 net-zero emission goal of the

## USA [1].

Unprecedented growth of utility-scale solar energy (USSE) will require significant quantities of land conversion [4]. PV solar facilities require a large amount of land per unit of electricity generated (15.01 km[2] /TWhr land-use efficiency) relative to traditional energy sources (e. g., surface coal: 8.19 km[2] /TWhr, natural gas: 0.95 km[2] /TWhr; [5]), and as much as 41,700 km[2] – an area larger than the state of Connecticut – are needed for conversion to solar energy to meet decarbonization goals as part of a renewable energy future [1]. Hot deserts of the southwestern USA (Chihuahuan, Mojave, Sonoran, and San Joaquin Deserts [6], hereafter “Desert Southwest”) have high solar energy potential and are already experiencing alteration of some intact natural plant communities and habitats to utility-scale PV solar [7,8]. Desert Southwest ecosystems, with a capacity to generate more than 9 GW (GW) on over 300 km[2] of land [9]. As of July 2023, an additional 15.4 GW worth of solar development on over 530 km[2] of land was undergoing environmental review [9]. However, many more USSE facilities in the Desert Southwest occur or may occur on other public and private lands, including in both previously disturbed and undisturbed areas.

When considering all USSE projects in the Desert Southwest, solar energy development is a new frontier in land-use with largely unquantified effects on desert plants, wildlife, and ecosystem processes. Early studies on the effects of solar energy were largely limited to documenting wildlife mortality caused by PV panels (e.g., collisions), solar flux from CSP (e.g., burns), and associated onsite infrastructure (e.g., entanglement in fencing and drowning in ponds) [10,11]. Recent reviews identify numerous types of local environmental effects related to USSE development and operation that, if not mitigated, influence various species by inducing: direct mortality, vegetation damage, soil disturbance, destruction and modification of habitat, emission of fugitive dust, light and noise pollution, generation of electromagnetic fields, alteration of hydrology and microclimate, water pollution and soil contamination, and water consumption in water-limited areas [7,12]. USSE facilities can also create habitat for species that benefit from human-induced environmental changes [13]. Emerging studies have estimated wider-ranging environmental effects caused by fences and energy transmission corridors and substations related to USSE [14]. These spatially extensive effects of USSE facilities include habitat fragmentation, changes in albedo and temperature, and barriers to movement and gene flow [7,15]. Larger-scale assessments are beginning to include some off-site effects related to construction material acquisition, processing, and transportation, as well as increases in wildfire potential [7]. USSE disturbance and related environmental effects can be both cumulative and interactive, and it is often difficult to determine cause and effect relationships of solar development and operation on plants and wildlife.

Nevertheless, synthesizing existing empirical results and developing predictions about potential responses of species and guilds to USSE development based on known responses determined by functional and life-history traits can help guide land management. The present study summarizes existing knowledge and uses morphological, phenological, physiological, reproductive, behavioral, and life-history traits (hereafter “traits”), as well as broader disturbance response strategies, to predict how species or guilds may respond to USSE disturbance and mitigation actions. Although the focus is primarily on utility-scale facilities that use PV panels due to their dominance in USSE solar energy growth projections, CSP, wind energy, and other large-scale disturbances are occasionally referenced when relevant for species and guilds that have not yet been extensively studied. The trait framework is applied to case studies with species and guilds of conservation concern: rare plants, invasive plants, desert shrubs, invertebrates, lizards, desert tortoises, birds, bats, ungulates, and kit foxes. Finally, broad mitigation strategies are reviewed with the goal of informing long-term planning and management decisions at USSE facilities.

## **2. Methods**

## _2.1. Framework to understand responses of species and guilds to USSE disturbance_

Predicting responses of desert plants, wildlife, and ecosystems to disturbances associated with PV USSE development and subsequent mitigation actions requires context about site history and the disturbance types created by development. For example, the direction and magnitude of species’ responses will depend upon: pre-construction land-use (i.e., agricultural, urban, or undisturbed natural lands) [4], siting decisions and build-out designs that avoid sensitive resources (e. g., washes) [16], and site preparation and construction methods (i.e.,

soil grading, vegetation removal) [16]. While USSE facilities are a relatively novel land-use, many of the disturbance types in the Desert Southwest created by their development and operation have been studied in other contexts [17]. Previous studies have identified specific disturbance types related to the construction and operation of USSE facilities, as well as environmental effects that occur as a result of those disturbance types [12,13]. However, as Moore O’Leary et al. [13] highlight, much remains unknown about the way these anthropogenic disturbance types and environmental effects will influence species of concern.

This review presents a framework (Fig. 1A) that builds on previous work by linking USSE disturbance types and environmental effects as direct and indirect drivers of species and guild responses. Direct effects of USSE development, when the disturbance itself influences the species response, are distinct from indirect effects of USSE development, when the species responses occur through environmental conditions that are modified by USSE disturbance. Construction methods and mitigation efforts that are used at USSE facilities can buffer disturbances and environmental effects and may be important determinants of species responses.

In the Desert Southwest, the traditional method of construction is blading vegetation and grading the soil surface (“Blade and Grade”) [12]. This method is currently the most widely used, with the greatest potential effects to species and guilds (Fig. 1B). An alternative to this method is a construction method that reduces destruction of vegetation and soil stability by driving over and crushing (“Drive and Crush” site preparation, per [18]) the plants and soils in areas that are unavoidable for solar infrastructure installation (Fig. 1C) while leaving some areas undisturbed. This method results in more intact vegetation since many desert plants are not damaged, and some of those that are crushed may regenerate. In addition, other mitigation efforts to reduce direct and indirect effects to plants and wildlife include fencing that allows certain species to pass under or through it and vegetation preservation or restoration (Fig. 1C).

The framework links the disturbance types induced by USSE facility construction and operation to environmental effects and species’ responses determined by traits and response strategies (Fig. 1A). By describing the responses of studied species to USSE development through their traits and strategies, predictions can be made for other species with known traits and response strategies, but which have not been studied in a USSE context.

## _2.2. Predicting plant and wildlife response through traits_

Previous research has found that traits, and related response strategies, are useful for predicting how species and guilds will respond to disturbance [19,20]. Traits include morphological, phenological, physiological, reproductive, and behavioral characteristics that are measurable and can be linked to performance, as well as life-history traits that can inform the vulnerability of life stages to disturbance and shifts in environmental conditions [21–23]. Plasticity, defined here as phenotypic flexibility within a trait, can influence the disturbance response for many species [24] and determine whether they persist. In some cases, traits on their own best predict a response. In other cases, traits can be grouped together into broader response strategies to predict how plants and wildlife may respond to USSE disturbance (Table 1).

Three response strategies (Table 1) are adapted and simplified from the urban ecology and wildlife literature [25,26] to include responses to USSE disturbance more broadly: avoid, tolerate, and exploit. Avoidant species avoid the disturbance, partially or entirely, to forestall negative effects of USSE disturbance types. They are not persistent in USSE areas and decline if disturbance cannot be avoided. Avoidant wildlife typically has narrow or inflexible ecological niches that make them vulnerable to disturbance, such as specific habitat requirements and specialized diets. Because of this, they will typically circumvent disturbance if they can and use alternative more suitable areas. Avoidance can also refer to

## **3. Results: species and guild case studies**

## _3.1. Plants_

## _3.1.1. Rare plants_

There are numerous causes of rarity in desert plants, and these causes can influence how a rare species might respond to USSE development [27]. Many rare species have narrow niches and/or occur in a limited geographic area, reproduce from long-lived seeds stored in the soil seedbank, and rely on specialized relationships with pollinators, all of which make them avoidant of disturbances like USSE development.

The diverse topography and soils of the Desert Southwest provide a multitude of habitats within which plant species have evolved. Many rare plants in the region occur in unique soil types such as gypsum or serpentine soils [28–30], and in topographical features such as low-relief washes [31]. However, soil destabilization, grading, and compaction during USSE site preparation can disturb specialized niches and disrupt specialized cues associated with topographical and edaphic diversity. For example, Mojave woolly sunflower ( _Eriophyllum mohavenses_ ) is a rare, annual forb that specializes in caliche soils and was found to be more sensitive to environmental variation than a closely related common species, woolly daisy ( _Eriophyllum wallacei_ ) [32]. Similarly, Las Vegas bearpoppy ( _Arctomecon californica;_ Fig. 2 _)_ is a rare perennial that specializes in gypsum soils, and the dissolution of gypsum can release sulfate ions that may contribute to _A. californica_ germination cues [33]. Disturbance that disrupts these specialized niches and cues, such as soil destabilization during USSE site preparation, is predicted to decrease the persistence of rare species that rely on edaphic, topographic, and geologic diversity.

For example, Mojave woolly sunflower was found to have relatively higher survival in the soil seed bank across all solar microsites compared to the closely related common species woolly daisy [34], indicating the importance of this seed reservoir. Although rare species that rely on persistence in the soil seed bank can avoid disturbance to some degree, they are predicted to be particularly vulnerable to USSE construction that involves expansive removal of topsoil and destabilization of soils. Prior to USSE construction, aboveground field studies can identify sensitive species, but these surveys often miss rare plants that are only present as seeds in the soil. When rare plant populations are identified prior to soil disturbance, mitigation such as creating protected patches may help to maintain populations, but the risk of loss of genetic diversity remains (e.g., Ref. [35]).

Habitat loss from USSE development has been found to reduce pollinators [18] (section 2.2.1) with implications for rare plants, many of which are self-incompatible and rely on specialized, co-evolved relationships with pollinators for reproduction. Therefore, rare plants with specialized pollinator requirements are predicted to be particularly vulnerable to USSE disturbance. For example, Peirson’s milkvetch ( _Astragalus magdalenae_ var. _peirsonii)_ is only found on the Algodones sand dunes in southeast California, is self-incompatible, and requires pollination by one species of native bee – all of which has made it particularly vulnerable to disturbance [36]. These specialized reproduction relationships are known for some rare plants, but are lacking for many other rare plants, complicating the ability to make accurate predictions about the effects of USSE development (e.g., Ref. [26]).

While most rare Desert Southwest plants are annuals, there are some rare perennial species. Perennial species may have more tolerance to USSE disturbance such as vegetation mowing, (e.g., Mojave milkweed [ _Asclepias nyctaginifolia]_ ) [35], but longer-term disturbances such as altered environmental conditions under PV panels are predicted to have negative effects. For example, Mojave milkweed decreases seed production in response to the altered microclimate beneath experimental solar panels [31], which could have negative effects on their long-term persistence in the seedbank. Additionally, shading and increased water stress, as would be experienced beneath PV panels, decreases cardenolide content, an important chemical defense in the rare Mojave milkweed [37] _._ A decrease in chemical defenses due to solar panel microsites, coupled with increased herbivory and/or granivory pressure in solar facilitates as a result of food web disruption [31], could leave these perennial plants more vulnerable to herbivory [38].

## _3.1.2. Invasive plants_

Invasive plants can exploit USSE disturbances because they often enter an ecosystem and/or spread following disturbances that create available niche space. During USSE construction and operation, practices that disturb soil and remove vegetation, such as blading and bulldozing, open up space and resources for invasive species to colonize and spread. Invasive annual grasses have been shown to increase following disturbance at wind farms compared to surrounding areas [39], and soil disturbance from blading and bulldozing in Mojave Desert solar developments led to the invasion by Mediterranean grass ( _Schismus_ spp.) [16].

Traits that enable invasive species to have an exploiter response strategy in disturbed areas include accelerated phenologies and large investments in reproduction [40,41]. For example, invasive bromes ( _Bromus_ spp.) and Mediterranean grass green-up earlier than many native plants in the Mojave Desert [42], taking advantage of cool-season precipitation before other species. Similarly, Sahara mustard ( _Brassica tournefortii_ ) is rapidly expanding in arid and semi-arid areas of the Desert Southwest, in part due to its rapid phenological development under a range of environmental conditions [43]. Large investments in reproduction also help invasive species become established and spread [44]. Invasive species often have prolific vegetative reproduction and high propagule pressure [45,46]. High propagule pressure, in particular,

may increase genetic variation to avoid inbreeding depression and allow for rapid selection of more successful genotypes in recently invaded areas [47]. This trait also allows for greater seed dispersal, increasing the chances of a seed landing somewhere suitable for recruitment. Although invasive species’ seeds tend to be relatively short-lived (e.g., Ref. [48]), their large numbers can still overwhelm native species in the seed bank [49]. These traits allow invasive species to exploit areas with soil disturbance, benefiting from USSE development.

Morphological traits such as high root to shoot ratios can increase the ability of invasive species to uptake water and nutrients [50–52]. Invasive species also tend to have lower leaf mass per unit area compared to native species, indicating thin, short-lived leaves that represent a low-resource investment [53,54]. By investing less in leaves, growing quickly, and completing their lifecycle rapidly, invasive species are opportunistic and able to capitalize with a high reproductive output when favorable conditions occur. While these advantages are not specific to USSE development, they contribute to the overall success of some invasive species to spread following disturbance.

Disturbed areas are not the only invasible landscapes in the Desert Southwest. There is also evidence of invasive species outcompeting native species in undisturbed, natural areas with more resources, such as beneath native perennial plant canopies [55]. Previous studies have found that invasive annual richness and biomass were driven more by microsite (based on soil moisture and N availability) than by disturbance [56,57], and some species, such as red brome ( _Bromus rubens_ ), are more likely to invade these resource-rich microsites than plant interspaces [58]. These studies suggest that, at least in some places, microsite may be as important as disturbance for predicting invasion [57]. USSE construction that removes perennial vegetation is likely to homogenize soil resources, including available nitrogen, across the landscape, potentially disadvantaging species that thrive in fertile islands. However, PV panels may create new areas with higher soil moisture below drip lines during operation of USSE facility, to the potential advantage of opportunistic invasive species such as red brome.

Invasive species also have high trait plasticity, further advantaging their exploiter response strategy. Plasticity and/or rapid evolution in phenology, morphology, and physiology enable invasive species to tolerate a wide variety of environmental conditions and to track and match altered conditions such as those that occur following USSE disturbance. A broad review found that invasive species have more phenotypic plasticity than native species in response to resource availability, but this plasticity did not always confer a fitness advantage, particularly under low-resource scenarios [59]. However, there may be a fitness advantage in areas where USSE disturbs vegetation and soil, and panels create microsites; many of the traits predicted to be advantageous in these areas are the same traits in which invasive species had more phenotypic plasticity: water-use efficiency, biomass, root biomass, root to shoot ratio, and nutrient-use efficiency [59]. In the Desert Southwest, many invasives species, including Sahara mustard [60] and cheatgrass ( _Bromus tectorum_ ) [61] have been found to have intraspecific variation in the timing of germination and flowering across populations in their invasive ranges, suggesting the ability to rapidly align these important traits with their environment. Like phenology, invasive species show high variation in important morphological traits, enabling them to succeed in diverse environments [62], while short-lived and inexpensive tissues allow invasive species to track limited resources, such as precipitation, through time [53]. Similarly, there is evidence that invasive species can rapidly adapt resource acquisition traits to match variation in resource availability [63], as is expected under solar panels with reduced light and precipitation.

Due to their dominant seasonal rainfall patterns, the Sonoran and Chihuahuan Deserts have more summer perennial invasive species, such as buffelgrass ( _Pennisetum ciliare_ ) and lovegrasses ( _Eragrostis_ spp.), while winter annual invasives are more widespread in the Mojave and San Joaquin Deserts. Across their invaded ranges, invasive plants create numerous ecological problems including increasing wildfire frequency

and displacing native vegetation, thereby reducing food for herbivores [64,65]. Minimizing the conditions that are predicted to promote invasive species colonization and spread (e.g., by using Drive and Crush disturbance methods instead of Blade and Grade), may reduce negative ecological outcomes.

## _3.1.3. Desert shrubs_

The direct effects of USSE facilities on desert shrubs depend on the methods of construction, operation, and vegetation management. The cover and height of creosote bush ( _Larrea tridentata_ ), a dominant shrub that spans the Desert Southwest, and other perennials were lower in bladed treatments compared to mowed and untreated areas of a Desert Southwest solar facility [16]. Large disturbances and cumulative effects of impermeable surfaces within facilities that divert water away from shrubs through runoff and overland flow will likely decrease their abundances [66]. The loss of desert perennial cover decreases habitat connectivity and accelerates land degradation [67]. Shrublands that experience the most severe levels of disturbance generally take the longest to recover, especially if the shrubs are long-lived [68].

When construction and vegetation management methods preclude the direct loss of shrubs in the Desert Southwest – such as using Drive and Crush methods – there are several traits that indicate shrub tolerance and potential vulnerability to the indirect effects of USSE facilities. Construction activities and PV panels change the amount and distribution of soil moisture within a USSE facility. Shrub roots are predicted to follow water availability, to the extent possible, becoming more developed in areas where water can accumulate or be retained, including under the driplines of PV panels and low microtopographic areas created by construction activity within the array. Many shrubs have deep roots that increase their extraction of water in the soil profile [69], buffering them from the loss of soil moisture directly under PV panels. Shrub roots can also span large horizontal distances [70], which may be extended even further to avoid the competitive pressure of neighbors [71]. Ogle and Reynolds [72] demonstrate high variability in the spatial distribution and density of roots of creosote bush, reflecting uptake of different precipitation event sizes. A high root to shoot ratio in desert shrubs [73] can allow continued water uptake and reallocation of carbon to aboveground canopies that may become damaged due to construction or mowing, trimming, and other vegetation maintenance within USSE facilities.

However, shrubs that are more shallow-rooted and have more fine roots directly below the canopy, including the drought deciduous white bursage ( _Ambrosia dumosa_ ) in the Mojave and Sonoran Deserts, may not be able to follow changing water availability [74]. Collectively, these results indicate that desert shrubs with expansive and dynamic root systems are predicted to maintain extraction of soil moisture even with changes in the amount and distribution of soil moisture caused by construction activities and PV panels within a USSE facility [75], while shrubs with smaller and less dynamic root systems may experience stress due to decreased water availability.

In addition to altering soil moisture availability, PV panels can provide shading, cooling, and increased humidity [76]. Solar-tracking PV panels in the Northern Hemisphere rotate east to west throughout the day, differentially exposing parts of shrub canopies to solar irradiance with implications for photosynthetic capacity; when panels are at horizontal positions at mid-day and provide more shade, there will likely be reduced heat loads that prevent leaf stress. In the absences of PV panels, shrub leaves are well-adapted to handle the high solar irradiance, heat load, and high atmospheric demand for moisture in the Desert Southwest and possess traits to minimize water loss including low specific leaf area, protective surfaces (e.g., waxy cuticle, hairs), and tolerance to high negative leaf water potentials [73]. However, there is evidence suggesting that shrubs may be able to alter leaf traits in altered light environments, including increasing specific leaf area and stomatal conductance [77]. Desert shrubs like desert holly ( _Atriplex hymenlytra_ ) have steep-angled leaves that reduce midday solar interception and heat

loads but maintain high interception when solar angles and vapor pressure deficits are low [77]. Shrub canopies can also be plastic in response to changes in light and water availability [78]. Creosote bush branches are oriented to maximize light interception in the early morning and may be pushed further outward with decreased stem angle relative to the ground [79] as light is intercepted by PV panels or other obstructions of light within the USSE facility. Although creosote bush had reduced canopy volume inside compared to outside a Desert Southwest USSE facility, the shrub had higher xylem water potentials, chlorophyll indices, and stem elongation inside the facility [80]. Triangle-leaf bursage ( _Ambrosia deltoidea_ ), a drought deciduous shrub, had higher leaf area and carbon fixation [81], while normally deciduous white bursage retained leaves and had a high level of stored carbohydrates [80], when grown under shaded compared to unshaded microsites. While desert shrubs are adapted to high light and water stress environments, there is evidence that they may have enough plasticity in leaf morphology and physiology to tolerate altered microclimates from PV solar.

## _3.2. Wildlife_

## _3.2.1. Invertebrates_

Invertebrate species are diverse and ubiquitous in deserts, outnumbering vascular plants and vertebrates by at least one order of magnitude [82]. Invertebrates can serve as useful bioindicators of land-use change in intricate yet vast Desert Southwest ecosystems because they may simultaneously respond to local environmental changes while being distributed across landscapes [83]. Relative to their abundance, diversity, and potential for bioindication in arid environments, little is known regarding response of invertebrates to USSE developments in deserts globally [84]. Models of potential habitat loss from land-conversion in the Mojave Desert for 10 _Ashmeadiella_ bee species indicated variable species responses and more direct habitat loss from urban sprawl than solar energy development [85]. However, native bee species richness and abundance in the Sonoran Desert was lower within solar facility footprints than adjacent undeveloped controls [86]. In the Mojave Desert, blading, mowing, and even undeveloped patches within a CSP facility decreased flower-visiting beetle and fly abundance and diversity relative to undeveloped controls [18]. At the same study site, researchers determined that bladed (i.e., bulldozed) treatments within the solar facility decreased ant abundance, species richness, Shannon Diversity Index, and functional richness relative to adjacent undeveloped controls, but undeveloped patches and mowed treatments did not [87]. Taken together, these findings suggest that pollinators may avoid areas with USSE development in deserts, whereas ants are tolerant of some less-intensive solar energy development.

Arid regions generally support the highest bee diversity globally [88], and the Mojave and Sonoran Deserts likely harbor the greatest diversity of solitary bees in the United States [89,90]. Saul-Gershenz et al. [86] determined that 76 % of bee species sampled in and around solar facilities in the Sonoran Desert nested in the ground. The habitat specificity of ground-nesting species suggests disturbance avoidance, and these species are likely to be negatively affected by USSE buildout, as construction often compacts and cools soils [84,91]. Additionally, reduction of floral resources (e.g., cacti, [16]) associated with USSE development may have deleterious effects on species that have evolved specific habitat requirements and pollen specialization [89,92]. Reductions in the abundance and diversity of pollinators from solar energy development in deserts may lead to cascading effects on biodiversity, including loss of valuable and rare plant species dependent on insect pollination for reproduction [18].

Apart from pollination, countless desert invertebrates maintain tightly coupled connections with soils and plants via behaviors such as burrowing, herbivory, and granivory [93]. For example, scorpions are major components of desert ecosystems and spend most of their time in burrows [94]. Since burrowing suggests an avoidance strategy,

disruption of surface soils from USSE site preparation could lead to habitat loss and mortality of scorpions and other invertebrate burrowers similar to that of fossorial vertebrates in deserts (see sections 3.2.2 and 3.2.3). As previously mentioned, USSE development in the Mojave Desert may affect the distribution, genetics, and growth of endemic Mojave milkweed ( _Asclepias nyctaginifolia_ ) [35,95], which, in turn, is a host plant for queen butterflies ( _Danaus gilippus thersippus_ ) [96,97]. As outlined above, intensive site preparation for USSE development may lead to increases in invasive grasses (e.g., Mediterranean grasses.; [16]) that increase wildfire intensity and frequency in the Desert Southwest [64]; invasive grass fire cycles can reduce desert ant species richness and diversity [98]. Given the rich co-evolution of insect-plant interactions in deserts (e.g., extrafloral nectaries and ants; [99]), removal of vegetation for USSE development may lead to unintended consequences affecting ecological processes [17].

The life histories, and thus traits, of most desert invertebrates have been and may remain unknown [100], and deserts continue to be a neglected biome for insect studies (e.g., Ref. [96]). Some progress has been made to understand terrestrial invertebrate response to USSE development in the Desert Southwest, with more studies underway, yet effects of altered hydrology from solar facility construction (see Ref. [13]) on aquatic invertebrates (e.g., brachiopod crustaceans, aquatic insects) of the Desert Southwest may be large [101] and remain empirically untested. Research on invertebrate community responses to USSE development in the Desert Southwest can elucidate “bottom-up” ecological mechanisms that inform adaptive management for desert ecosystems and all wildlife therein [84,102].

## _3.2.2. Lizards_

There is a paucity of information related to desert lizard vulnerability to USSE development. Undoubtedly, desert lizards will be affected by habitat loss related to USSE developments as seen with habitat loss related to other anthropogenic disturbances [17]: however, these effects might be mitigated, to some degree, through siting choices and the retention of onsite vegetation. One study reported that blunt-nosed leopard lizards ( _Gambelia silus_ ) occupied PV facilities with vegetation [103], suggesting short-term ecological compatibility – thus tolerance of some USSE disturbances is possible. More long-term research on the effects of PV facilities, including habitat loss, fragmentation, onsite habitat suitability (e.g., basal resources), and ecological and physiological processes, could determine whether desert lizard species truly are tolerant of USSE development.

Like many reptiles, desert lizards are heliotherms, regulating their body temperature behaviorally by moving between sunlight and shaded cover [104]. Indirect effects of PV arrays on local and regional temperatures are predicted to exert some influence on lizard thermoregulation and behavior. PV solar panel arrays have been implicated as contributing to local nighttime temperature increases [105] as well as modeled regional afternoon temperature increases [106] via a “heat island effect”. However, others have demonstrated that PV installations can form “cool islands” due to shading from panels and removal of electrical energy from their footprint. The cooling effect can be up to 2.3[◦] C and detectable up to 730 m away from the nearest 100 m buffer on the edge of the facility [91].

Shaded microhabitats under the PV panels could conceivably be beneficial to some species due to PV-induced temperature differences. Most species that evolved in the Desert Southwest use native shrubs for shaded cover, so “benefits” from panel shade are likely not necessary for their continued survival. Whether or not lizard species have the behavioral plasticity to substitute panels for shrubs remains to be seen.

Some lizards like the chuckwalla ( _Sauromelus obesus_ ) exploit warm microhabitats, such as those that may be created by higher regional temperatures attributed to the larger footprint of PV solar development [106]. Chuckwallas are predicted to expand their range into warmer regions of the Mojave and Sonoran deserts under modeled climate warming scenarios [107], and regional warming from PV could speed up

this expansion. However, other research predicts that warming (from current climate projections) will lead to declines in lizard diversity in the Desert Southwest via physiological models [103]. Given the diversity of lizard species in the Desert Southwest and their variable life histories it is difficult to accurately predict species-specific responses to USSE development without additional research.

## _3.2.3. Desert tortoises_

Agassiz’s desert tortoises ( _Gopherus agassizii_ ; Fig. 2) are a conservation-reliant flagship species in the Mojave and Sonoran Deserts, and emblematic of the tension between conservation of desert habitats and solar energy development [108]. Cause and effect relationships of USSE development on tortoise populations are unknown because before-after-control-impact studies are lacking [7]. Given that some recent PV facilities are being constructed to retain some intact native vegetation (e.g., Drive and Crush), a pilot study is underway to investigate the compatibility of desert tortoises within a vegetated PV facility with wildlife-friendly fencing after construction. If compatible, those PV facilities would not represent a total loss of desert tortoise habitat, but long-term monitoring could inform demographic effects.

The standard mitigation technique for USSE development since 1986 [109] has been to translocate tortoises from the footprint of USSE development into another area, sometimes far away. This strategy has been controversial. Translocation of reptiles, including desert tortoises, is not always successful and has been criticized for many years [110, 111]. In addition, long-term data (e.g., _>_ 5 years: [112]) are not available to verify success in such long-lived species as desert tortoises (up to about 50 years in the wild) [113]. Research on tortoises moved because of USSE development has focused on body temperature, condition, growth, and mortality of translocated tortoises [114]; survival [112]; and movements [115]: all based on short-term studies.

Tortoises tend to be disturbance avoiders, possessing a number of traits (e.g., diet of diverse forb species, susceptibility to road mortality) that make them vulnerable to disturbance, including USSE-related translocation. Translocated tortoises may experience high mortality, especially during periods of drought [116,117]. They have also been shown to make extensive movements in the first year [118], before settling into their new home ranges, potentially increasing the risk of road mortality. There is also increased disease outbreak risk following translocation and intermingling of sick and healthy tortoises [119]. More troubling is a demonstrated lack of breeding by translocated male tortoises with resident or translocated females [120].

The success of translocation efforts is only one concern relative to recovery of threatened tortoise populations. Habitat loss and degradation is a major challenge for tortoise conservation and as many as 700 km[2] of tortoise habitat may be lost to solar energy development [121] on top of previous losses [17] if not mitigated (i.e., leaving onsite native vegetation and wildlife friendly fencing). Habitat fragmentation due to USSE development may disrupt genetic linkages of desert tortoise in the Mojave Desert as well [122]. Even if tortoise habitat remains, temperature changes within habitat patches could alter tortoises environmental sex determination. For example, increased regional temperatures associated with USSE facilities [105] may result in production of only female hatchlings and no males [123].

Desert tortoises are slow to recover from population declines for any reason because of their life-history traits of late maturity, long-lives, and relatively small annual reproductive output. Even before widespread USSE development in tortoise habitat, range-wide populations declined an estimated 37 % from 2004 to 2014 [124] due to other factors. The longevity of adults also contributes to the “perception of persistence” of populations [125], even if they are no longer producing recruitable offspring. It will be difficult or impossible to determine the ultimate success of translocation studies without long-term monitoring commensurate with the longevity of tortoises.

## _3.2.4. Birds_

Avian solar challenges include direct fatality risks associated with solar infrastructure (e.g., panel collision) and indirect effects through habitat loss. Avian remains (e.g., carcasses and feather spots) have been reported at multiple USSE PV facilities, although studies have been largely confined to southern California [14,126–128]. Eighty-six avian species from 17 Orders, largely from Passeriformes (55 % of remains) and Columbiformes (17 % of remains), were identified [126], and the majority of the remains that could be identified were small-bodied species [14]. The most commonly detected species were mourning doves ( _Zenaida macroura_ ), western meadowlarks ( _Sturnella neglecta_ ) _,_ horned larks ( _Eremophila alpestris_ ) _,_ and house finches ( _Haemorphous mexicanus_ ) [126]. Several of these species share similar ecological traits including ground dwelling, regional abundance, or frequent association with anthropogenic structures [126].

Among the avian remains detected at USSE facilities in the Desert Southwest are wetland-oriented species, which collectively represent 14 % of remains [126,127]. These waterbirds possess specific habitat requirements, such as aquatic foraging, reproduction, and roosting. One explanation for the detection of these aquatic-habitat species, and other bird species, is the _Lake Effect_ Hypothesis, which posits that some avian species could perceive the polarized light emissions from PV USSE facilities as a body of water [129,130], increasing collision and stranding risks (i.e., species that require water to take off) [10]. However, there is little published information supporting the _Lake Effect_ Hypothesis for avian species other than remains and observations of avian species including water-habitat species detected on site [14,126,127]. Kosciuch et al. [127] observed no maladaptive behaviors (e.g., landing attempts or circling) of water-habitat species during diurnal surveys at USSE facilities. It should be noted that various stakeholder groups have made progress in understanding mechanisms, such as sensory and behavioral aspects of species, associated with the _Lake Effect_ hypothesis [14]. However, understanding of avian species being attracted to PV facilities is currently limited, and likely influenced by onsite and landscape context, which is often not included or analyzed in studies.

Avian fatalities within USSE facilities have been associated with collisions with panels, electrical lines, buildings, electrocution, predation, entanglement (e.g., netting and fencing), and drowning [14,126]. However, most cause of deaths are unknown (~60 %; [126]), so cannot be attributed to USSE infrastructure or background mortality. Various stakeholder groups express concern over avian collisions with panels [131]; however, more avian fatalities are associated with non-panel infrastructure collisions (21 %, e.g., electrical lines and buildings) than PV panels (16 %) - the most dominant feature of the USSE PV solar facility [126]. Fatality rate estimates are commonly reported in the literature that are standardized by megawatt (MW) per year to facilitate comparisons among facilities. These rates varied considerably among facilities (0.1–9.26 fatalities/MW/year [126]; 2.13 to 28.64 fatalities/MW/year; [14]), suggesting onsite and landscape conditions might influence fatality rates. Other conditions that may influence variation in fatality rates are differences in data collection procedures as there is no standardization among facilities, and whether background mortality rates (i.e., natural mortality, such as predation or disease) are incorporated into the estimates [14,132].

Population-level or cumulative effect associated with USSE facilities have been reported using demographic models [133] and estimating avian losses associated with annual fatality rates and habitat loss (i.e., nesting sites) in the Desert Southwest [14]. Conkling et al. [133] reported western yellow-billed cuckoo ( _Coccyzus americanus occidentalis_ ), willow flycatcher ( _Epidonax traillii_ ), American white pelican ( _Pelecanus erthrorhynchos_ ), and western grebe ( _Aechmophorus occidentalis_ ) populations (i.e., local and/or non-local) are vulnerable to increases in annual fatalities associated with USSE facilities, which included both PV and CSP. Smallwood [14] estimated 90,811 avian nest sites in southern California were displaced or destroyed due to solar facility developments by 2020, and nearly 7.5 million individual birds (i.e., based

upon breeding capacity and annual offspring production) will be lost due to habitat destruction over a 25-year period (i.e., operational lifespan of USSE facilities). In Imperial County, California, roughly 16 km[2] of burrowing owl ( _Athene cunicularia_ ; Fig. 2) habitat has been lost to solar development, which equates to an annual loss of approximately 1000 burrowing owls, and in combination with fatalities rate estimates, over 1300 burrowing owls could be lost annually [14]. However, burrowing owls are known to occupy seven USSE PV facilities in the San Joaquin Desert [103], indicating at least some tolerance to USSE PV facilities.

These avian studies [14,127,133] are coarse indicators of potential population-level effects related to USSE solar, and more long-term studies would help to quantify population dynamics further. For example, both studies assume additive and not compensatory effects from the USSE facilities and do not incorporate other demographic process, such as immigration, emigration, density-dependent responses, and reproduction within the USSE facilities. In the Desert Southwest, construction practices have often included the removal of all native vegetation, eliminating breeding, foraging, shelter, and migratory stop-over habitats of avian species [14]. However, new construction approaches (e.g., Drive and Crush) that leave vegetation between panel rows and elsewhere might provide some habitat for desert-dwelling avian species and ameliorate some habitat effects (see Ref. [103]). Whether or not bird species are able to tolerate or even exploit this habitat remains to be seen. Additionally, although not in the Desert Southwest, avian nests have been observed within USSE facilities’ infrastructure [134,135], and the greater sage-grouse ( _Centrocercus urophasianus_ ), a sensitive species to anthropogenic development, has been observed within a USSE facility, indicating at least some tolerance to USSE development for some bird species.

## _3.2.5. Bats_

Like birds, bats face fatality risks and habitat loss from USSE development; however, understanding of fatality risks and habitat loss for bats is poor as there is a lack of information related to solar-bat interactions in the Desert Southwest. There is one peer-reviewed publication reporting bat carcasses at three solar fatalities in southern California over several years [14]; therefore, any generalizations or extrapolation beyond these facilities must be done with caution as there is no onsite or landscape context associated with the data. Bat research at other renewable energy sites indicate that location, temperature, and landscape features are important predictors of fatalities [136].

Canyon bats ( _Parastrellus hesperus_ ), California myotis ( _Myotis californicus_ ), and Mexican free-tailed bats ( _Tadarida brasiliensis_ ) were the most commonly detected carcasses at USSE facilities (largely CSP), but Yuma myotis ( _Myotis yumanensis_ ), western small-footed myotis ( _Myotis ciliolabrum_ ), and pallid bats ( _Antrozous pallidus_ ) have also been detected in low numbers [14]. Interestingly, Mexican free-tailed bats represent over half of the fatalities (52.6 %) at wind facilities in the Desert Southwest (specifically, California and Nevada) [137], which might suggest a sensitivity to renewable energy developments or anthropogenic developments in general. However, bat fatality rate estimates are higher for parabolic trough (10.92 fatalities/MW/year) and tower CSP facilities (1.79 fatalities/MW/year) than a PV facility (0.46 fatalities/MW/year).

The cause of death of bats is usually unknown (i.e., approximately 80 %), limiting understanding of any causal mechanisms or vulnerability traits. At a USSE CSP facility, carcasses have been found associated with evaporation ponds, power blocks, fencing, and mirrors [14], suggesting that power blocks and fencing may also pose a risk to bats at PV facilities.

As a group, bats possess life-history traits (e.g., long-lived, low fecundity) that are sensitive to changes in adult mortality [138] – an avoidant strategy. Any increase in mortality could have population-level effects to species; however, no study has investigated the long-term population trends related to solar-bat interactions. Smallwood [14]

predicted annual bat fatalities using his fatality rate estimates and California’s installed PV capacity at 716 bats (95 % confidence intervals - 124–1221) annually. More research would improve understanding of long-term population trends related to the increase of bat fatalities and habitat loss due to direct and indirect effects of solar facilities in the Desert Southwest.

## _3.2.6. Desert bighorn sheep and other ungulates_

Ungulates exhibit seasonal migratory movements in response to variation in environmental factors, especially food and water availability, on local and regional scales – greater distances than many other species [139]. Traditional migratory routes can be lost or threatened by barriers including roads and urban and USSE developments. Ungulate species, such as mule deer ( _Odocoileus hemionus_ ) and pronghorn antelope ( _Antilocapra americana_ ), have previously been found to avoid oil and gas development facilities or expend a high amount of energy to move through areas developed for energy extraction [140,141]. It is unknown whether USSE will trigger the same avoidance of infrastructure. However, fencing around USSE facilities is likely to cause barrier effects to both resident and migratory populations of pronghorn antelope [142].

Specific studies that have been published on the response of desert bighorn sheep ( _Ovis canadensis nelsoni_ ; Fig. 2) to solar energy facilities in the Desert Southwest are lacking. The lack of focused studies on the effect of USSE facilities as barriers to sheep is due in part to the assumption that desert bighorn sheep do not utilize the relatively flat desert valleys where USSE development occurs. Desert sheep populations have a naturally fragmented distribution mostly restricted to isolated mountain ranges with steep terrain and sparse vegetation. However, desert sheep research demonstrates that they use intermountain valley habitat more often than was previously thought [143], including places where USSE projects have been planned or constructed [144]. Reviewing information on the effects of various other human disturbances on movement and genetic connectivity provides an opportunity to make predictions that are ultimately hypotheses for how USSE development might affect sheep populations, as previous research has done [84].

Population genetic structure has been observed in desert sheep populations, even in contiguous mountain ranges. Movement between mountain ranges allows for gene flow among populations but only if the span of land unsuitable for habitat is narrow, and there are limited physical barriers erected by humans that restrict movements such as large roads [145], fences in general [146], and presumably solar facilities that are fenced so that sheep and other ungulates cannot pass through [142].

Over 30 years ago, Bleich et al. [143] said: “ _Given the heretofore unrecognized vagility of mountain sheep, we argue that existing corridors of “nontraditional” habitat connecting mountain ranges be given adequate conservation consideration_ .” The point about maintaining connectivity among populations was reiterated by Epps et al. [147]. Without such consideration, desert sheep populations are predicted to be negatively affected as USSE facilities cover more of the desert valleys between mountain ranges blocking movements among populations. Based on current scientific understanding this will contribute to loss of genetic diversity and reduce or eliminate the ability to recolonize previously occupied habitats [147].

Onsite vegetation management practices, such as weed control, revegetation and restoration, and mechanical mowing is sometimes supplemented by sheep grazing, allowing for habitat for kit foxes and other wildlife [103,148]. For example, most demographic and ecological data did not differ from kit fox populations at solar facilities and non-solar sites [103]. The probability of survival ranged 0.65 to 0.84 on solar facilities and did not differ from non-solar sites (i.e., 0.38–1.0). Solar infrastructure (i.e., fencing and panels) is hypothesized to reduce kit fox predation by excluding larger mammalian predators and provide refugia from aerial predators [103]. Furthermore, most kit fox mortalities occurred outside the fencing of the facilities, and no fatalities haven been associated with construction and operation of the facilities [103]. Reproductive attributes (i.e., reproductive success and litter size) and body mass did not differ between PV facilities and non-solar sites, suggesting solar facilities and adjacent habitats provide enough prey resources for growth, fat storage, and reproduction. One ecological attribute that did differ between solar facilities and non-solar sites is home range size [103]. Two of the kit fox populations occupying solar facilities had larger home ranges than non-solar sites. Often home range size is inversely related to habitat quality for kit foxes, and the two sites with suppressed home ranges were constructed on agricultural lands or low-quality habitat [103], which might decrease prey density at the facility and within the surrounding landscape.

## **4. Discussion**

## _4.1. Mitigation strategies_

The plant and wildlife case studies demonstrate that USSE disturbance types during construction and operation can have direct and indirect effects on species and guilds in the Desert Southwest (summarized in Table 2). Many of the predicted effects on species and guilds are negative. However, there are a variety of site-level management actions that may mitigate the impacts of USSE, in addition to the species-specific mitigation actions mentioned in the previous case studies. The mitigation hierarchy from the U.S. National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) provides a decision-making hierarchy to mitigate the effects of solar energy development on sensitive resources, including species and guilds (Fig. 3). There are three hierarchical levels – avoidance, minimization, and restoration or offsetting – which have successfully been applied to other forms of renewable energy development (e.g., wind) [149].

## _4.3. Minimization_

In cases where sensitive or important natural areas supporting diverse species and guilds are not avoided, there are design, infrastructure, and management options to minimize the effects to environmental conditions and species in all phases of USSE development. Construction tactics that minimize disturbance to vegetation and soil, such as avoiding surface grading, using hand-crews to install panels instead of heavy machinery, or working around existing vegetation (i.e., “Drive and Crush” methods instead of blading vegetation), could be effective. At a landscape scale, leaving patches of undisturbed soils and vegetation can increase ecosystems services in USSE facilities [16,152], and could maintain hydrologic connectivity [101], serve as refugia or islands for recolonization [153], and reduce the negative impacts to habitat connectivity [e.g., 149], although these remain understudied. Minimization efforts can be taken as far as trying to maximize ecosystem services in tandem with energy generation, termed ‘ecovoltaics’ [154]. Species with tolerant or avoidant response strategies are unlikely to see a net benefit from USSE development that occurs on intact ecosystems in the Desert Southwest, but the results in this review suggest ways that ecovoltaics may result in some neutral or positive effects, including reduced drought-stress [155] and the creation of diverse microclimates for certain plants [32]. Ecovoltaics does not address all disturbance types, including corridor loss which is key to ungulates and other wildlife guilds. In these cases, landscape-level conservation planning is likely to be more effective for minimization of adverse effects [156].

Other strategies to minimize negative effects to species and guilds include burying powerlines, using more efficient infrastructure (i.e., solar cells that capture more energy/area) that minimizes the development footprint, avoiding loud and disruptive machinery at critical times for wildlife, and minimizing mechanical or chemical treatments on vegetation. Several USSE facilities have successfully implemented wildlife-friendly fencing [103] and undisturbed buffer areas [16] as minimization strategies. Altering the layout of USSE infrastructure – such as the design of the panels, the distance between panels, or the panels mounted height – can influence environmental conditions within the facility (e.g., temperature, wind, and shading, as noted by Ref. [157]), and yet studies manipulating infrastructure layout to minimize environmental effects of USSE are lacking.

## _4.4. Restoration and offsetting_

The final level in the mitigation hierarchy is for situations where avoidance and mitigation are not possible or are ineffective, resulting in impacts to sensitive or important natural areas. In these cases, landscape-level compensation efforts for the effects of the development on species and guilds can be made. Species and guild responses that occur via environmental effects like habitat loss may be effectively mitigated through restoration. Unfortunately, native plant revegetation is notoriously difficult in desert environments and has low rates of success. Out-planting and transplanting typically have higher success rates than other restoration methods such as seeding [158,159]. USSE facilities may be particularly well-suited to transplanting, depending on the size of the area needed to revegetate, and the ability to salvage local plants prior to construction.

Soils can also be restored following USSE disturbance. Saving topsoil in heavily affected areas, using soil amendments, and recreating

microtopography and water catchment are all soil restoration techniques that could improve restoration outcomes [160–163]. Similarly, salvage biocrust restoration offers a lot of promise at USSE facilities that are being constructed on intact biocrust [164]. Shading and reduced evapotranspiration in solar panel microsites may benefit restoration efforts, as shading is an important condition for seedling survival for many species in the Desert Southwest [165–169] and has also been shown to increase biocrust establishment [170–172]. Species that are most likely to benefit from soil and plant restoration include species that are sensitive to habitat loss. When the effects to species and guilds cannot be mediated by restoration (for example, restrictions in desert big horn sheep migration), similar resources can be selected for preservation as offsets if they exist (such as comparable desert big horn sheep habitat corridors) [173].

## **5. Directions for future research and conclusions**

As this review highlights, there is currently a lack of information about how USSE will affect species and guilds throughout the world. These effects may be especially pronounced in already vulnerable Desert Southwest ecosystems, which occupy a region that favors rapid USSE expansion. Given the growing demand for solar energy development, it is critical to assess baseline ecological conditions and monitor impacts so that best management practices can be developed to mitigate the effects of USSE development on plants and wildlife. The framework presented in this review may be useful for bridging this knowledge gap and providing guidance for future sustainable development of USSE in the Desert Southwest and deserts globally.

USSE plays a pivotal role in reducing carbon emissions to mitigate climate change and ameliorate impacts to species and ecosystems. Accounting for climate-related effects in the absence of a renewable energy transition including USSE will allow for more accurate predictions of species and guild responses in the Desert Southwest [174]. Indeed, climate change also poses a conservation challenge, increasing the extinction risk of species and disrupting ecosystems [175]. In this context, USSE is an important part of conserving biodiversity (via climate change mitigation), while also posing a challenge to conservation of habitat through land-use change.

To balance USSE development with the conservation of plants and wildlife, this review indicates priorities for future research. Understanding impacts to species and guilds will depend on investigating direct (i.e., mortality) and indirect effects (i.e., altered microclimate) of USSE disturbance. While past research has largely focused on one of these effects, there is a lack of research that captures both, including through experimental approaches that test the impacts of alternative construction methods, site layouts, and maintenance practices. These studies can contribute to broader knowledge of the efficacy of mitigation efforts. While this review provides examples of USSE effects on species and guilds, studies that incorporate multiple plant and wildlife guilds, and interactions among them, can more comprehensively reveal cumulative responses. Studies on food webs, reproductive linkages, vegetation structural influences on habitat, and plant-animal interactions are critical to reveal the network of ecological effects created by USSE development. These studies also point to a lack of research on USSE effects at large spatial scales, including studies that assess effects across entire facilities, compare the responses of species and guilds among facilities, and examine the cumulative effects of multiple facilities.

This review highlights the utility of using traits and response strategies to predict the effects of USSE on species and guilds in the Desert Southwest (Table 2) as research catches up to the rapid pace of solar deployment in the Desert Southwest. While the best outcome for species in most cases would be to site solar energy on lands that are not crucial habitat, a key takeaway from this review is that there may be opportunities to minimize and mitigate disturbance during facility design, construction, and operation, and even to co-locate habitat and energy production (i.e., “ecovoltaics”; [154]). Species’ predicted responses vary

greatly depending on the specific type of disturbance and adopted mitigation measures (e.g., wildlife-friendly fencing and vegetation management), suggesting that facilities could be designed to maximize ecosystem services provided by important species or resources.

Species that exhibit plasticity in traits or have a broad ecological niche are predicted to survive and even take advantage of USSE disturbance. These include species and guilds that fall under the tolerate or exploit response strategies, respectively, though avoidant species can persist under certain circumstances. Their future viability will depend on whether their disturbance thresholds are exceeded by the USSE disturbance. Species with specific requirements and narrow niches are predicted to be more vulnerable to USSE disturbance. There are a number of promising mitigation strategies that could benefit species, although additional research would enable evaluation of mitigation efficacy.

This review suggests many linkages between USSE disturbance and traits or response strategies, which can serve as a starting point for empirical research to test the validity of these predictions. The Desert Southwest is in the midst of rapid growth in USSE development, and the effects of this land-use on species and guilds deserve far more research attention than has so far been received.
